original_question: For stadium-like billiards that contain marginally unstable periodic orbits, can one comprehensively characterize their dynamical and escape properties in terms of the reinjection dynamics of trajectories that leave and later return to the neighborhood of those periodic orbits?
target_in_paper: Problem 11.9 in Section 11.4, Defocusing and intermittent billiards: “Give a comprehensive characterisation of the dynamical (including escape) properties of marginally unstable periodic orbits in stadium-like billiards in terms of their reinjection dynamics.” ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s official formulation: it has the correct setting (stadium-like billiards), the correct objects (marginally unstable periodic orbits), the correct goal (a comprehensive characterization), and the correct emphasis on dynamical and escape properties being described through reinjection dynamics. Your gloss about trajectories leaving and later returning to the relevant region also matches the nearby discussion of orbits leaving the bouncing-ball region and being reinjected back. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))
missing_details: The paper frames this as an open problem, specifically Problem 11.9 in Section 11.4, not as a theorem or conjecture. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))

The immediate model behind the question is the stadium billiard’s bouncing-ball family, used as the canonical example of marginally unstable periodic orbits in this subsection. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))

The nearby context says that, in the stadium, trajectories leaving the bouncing-ball region are immediately reinjected back, and the reinjection angle is approximately described by an independent stochastic process. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))

The paper also notes that other reinjection mechanisms are possible, depending on the curvature of the boundary near the endpoints of the bouncing-ball orbits; this is part of the intended scope of the problem. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))

The phrase “including escape” is essential in the paper and is motivated by the immediately preceding open-stadium escape discussion, including Eq. (11.10) for the leading coefficient of tP(t). ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree restriction, nilpotency condition, or quantifier such as “for all sufficiently large m” is relevant here; the missing stand-alone data are geometric and dynamical, not algebraic. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))
refined_question: For stadium-like billiards whose intermittency is generated by bouncing-ball or, more generally, marginally unstable periodic orbits, can one give a comprehensive characterization of the resulting dynamical properties—including escape/survival behavior—in terms of the reinjection dynamics of trajectories that leave the bouncing-ball (or analogous marginally unstable) region and are reinjected into it? ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))
justification: The draft is a near paraphrase of Problem 11.9, so that is the exact target rather than a broader neighboring question. The surrounding discussion in Section 11.4 fixes the intended scope: the stadium is treated as a defocusing/intermittent billiard whose weaker statistical behavior comes from bouncing-ball or more general marginally unstable periodic orbits; the open stadium is discussed through Eq. (11.10); and the key mechanism singled out before Problem 11.9 is reinjection, with the stadium exhibiting immediate reinjection back into the bouncing-ball region and other reinjection laws depending on boundary curvature near the endpoints. ([people.maths.bris.ac.uk](https://people.maths.bris.ac.uk/~macpd/open/open.pdf))
